text: I never thought I would say this, but let's talk about the Mongolian matriarchy. So this lady claims that the Mongolian matriarchy was polygamous and women had multiple husbands as slaves. And as proof, she shows this old newspaper clipping. So let's figure out what this source actually is and whether the claim has any real historical support. As you guys may know that I am Kazakh, Kazakhs and Mongols are not the same people, but our histories are quite connected. The Kazakh Khans trace their lineage back to Genghis Khan and we share a similar nomadic steppe background. So this topic is quite interesting to me. But okay, now let's examine her proof. What she shows is not a historical study or even a direct report from researchers. It's an old newspaper article describing a radio lecture broadcast by a station in Hobart, Australia. The speaker was discussing Robert Brieffold's 1927 book, Them Others, which argued that all human societies had originally passed through a mother-centered or matriarchal phase, a sweeping theory that mainstream anthropology has since largely rejected. But the claim about Mongolia didn't even come directly from Brieffold's book. The speaker quoted another newspaper, The Mercury, which claimed a tribe had been discovered in Mongolia by Russian scientists. It was supposedly ruled by women and every woman had several husbands as absolute slaves. So which tribe? It doesn't say. Which Russian scientists? It doesn't say. So the evidence chain is an old newspaper reporting on a radio speaker quoting another newspaper which referred to unnamed scientists and an unnamed tribe. That proves that the story was printed. It doesn't prove that the story was true. And even if this unidentified tribe really existed, the article says a tribe in Mongolia. It doesn't say that Mongolian society generally operated this way. Turning one alleged tribe into the Mongolian matriarchy is already a massive leap. What we actually know about historical Mongol society is much less dramatic. Mongol society was predominantly patriarchal and patrilineal. Descent and clan identity generally passed through the male line. When plural marriage occurred, it was usually polygyny, wealthy men having multiple wives, not women keeping multiple husbands. But Mongol women did have considerable independence compared with women in many other societies of the period. They managed household and livestock, could control property and commercial activity, advised political leaders, and some elite widows even governed as regents. So yes, women could hold substantial economic and political power. But women having influence does not automatically make a society matriarchal. And it definitely does not prove that husbands were routinely kept as slaves. Could some isolated community have practiced polyandry? Possibly. Anthropologists have documented polyandrous unions in a small number of societies around the world. But this clipping gives us no reliable way to verify this particular story. And this is my problem with using history for gender war content. You cannot find one dramatic sentence in an old newspaper, remove every layer of uncertainty, turn an unidentified tribe into an entire civilization, and then present it as proof of how women naturally treated men. That isn't historical education. It's just a gender war fanfiction.
